# oorandom - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/oorandom/

## Expand description

A tiny, robust PRNG implementation.

More specifically, it implements a single GOOD PRNG algorithm,
which is currently a permuted congruential generator.  It has two
implementations, one that returns `u32` and one that returns
`u64`.  It also has functions that return floats or integer
ranges.  And that’s it.  What more do you need?

For more info on PCG generators, see http://www.pcg-random.org/

This was designed as a minimalist utility for video games. No promises are made about its quality, and if you use it for cryptography you will get what you deserve.

Works with `#![no_std]`, has no global state, no dependencies
apart from some in the unit tests, and is generally neato.

# oorandom 11.1.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/oorandom/latest

# oorandom

# What is this?

`oorandom` is a minimalistic pseudorandom number generator in Rust.  For
those times when the `rand` crate is just too big and you want something
a bit dumber.

More specifically, it implements ONE prng, which is currently a permuted
congruential generator (PCG).  It may change if something better comes
along, but that seems unlikely and will probably be a major version
bump.  It will give you `u32` or `u64`, and signed or floating-point
equivalents.  It is also `#[no_std]`.  Anything else is gravy.

Thanks to Lokathor for making
[ randomize](https://github.com/Lokathor/randomize), which inspired me
to do my own equivalent.

The name comes from my attempts to find a good way to pronounce
`/dev/urandom`.

Please direct questions, discussions and bugs to the [issue
tracker](https://todo.sr.ht/~icefox/oorandom).

# Why use `oorandom` instead of...

- `rand`--- `oorandom`is simpler and has zero choices you need to make. It also compiles in 1/10th the time and has a stable API.
- `getrandom`-- They solve different problems;- `getrandom`gives you whatever secure randomness the OS decides to give you, not a deterministic and seedable PRNG. It's generally a good idea to use- `getrandom`to seed this RNG though.
- `randomize`--- `randomize`used to be more complicated, but- `randomize`3.x is quite similar to- `oorandom`in functionality and design. Go for it.
- `rand_pcg`and- `rand_core`-- Yes you can take- `rand`apart into its pieces and use those individually, if you want to abandon having an all-in-one solution, still deal with the lack of stability in- `rand_core`and actually figure out which pieces you need. It works just fine. Seems more complicated than it needs to be though.
- `nanorand`--- `nanorand`uses the- [WyRand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash)PRNG algorithm, which is supposedly faster than PCG and at least as good quality. I haven't verified these claims, and I don't know of any- *really*thorough 3rd party investigation into them, though it apparently passes- [Dr. Lemire's tests](https://github.com/lemire/testingRNG). So for now I personally consider WyRand to be in the "trust but verify" level of quality. It's probably fine. Check back in 2027.
- `fastrand`-- Looks fine, uses the same algorithm as- `oorandom`. Made by the same people as the- `smol`async runtime, which may be good or bad for you. Does slightly more than- `oorandom`does, which may be good or bad for you. Use it if you like it.

# This is not...

This is not cryptographically secure, and if you use it for crypto you
will get what you deserve.  You are also in charge of choosing a useful
seed; the `getrandom` crate might be useful for that.

This is also not optimized to be stupidly fast, but is basically just
as fast as `rustc` feels like making it.  This means it is safe and robust
and portable and involves absolutely zero clever tricks.

# Usage

```
use oorandom;
```
If you want a nondeterministic seed, I recommend using the `getrandom` crate to produce one.

# License

MIT

# A brief history of random numbers

The usefulness of random numbers has been known for a long, long time to people who also knew how to use slide rules. If you wanted to do some math without the bother of coming up with all that pesky input data from the real world, you might as well just use any ol' random numbers, as long as there weren't any patterns in them to heck up the patterns you were trying to look at. So in the first half of the 20th century you had little old ladies named Edith spinning roulette wheels or pulling bingo balls out of baskets and writing the results down, which got assembled into giant tomes and published so that engineering schools could buy them and have giant tomes sitting on their shelves. Anyone who wanted some meaningless numbers could pull the tome down, flip it open to a presumably-random page, and there were all the random numbers anyone could want. The problem was solved, and life was good.

In late 1940's computers were invented, but they were far too big and
expensive to be put on the task of *intentionally* generating
nonsense, and things carried on as before.  If you needed random
numbers in a computer program, you just got a pretty young lady named
Mary to transcribe part of the book to punch cards for you.

Around the early 1960's computers got fast enough that Edith and Mary couldn't keep up with them, so they got downsized and replaced with more computers. To do this people came up with Linear Congruential Generators (LCG's), which could generate lots of numbers numbers that weren't really random, but sure looked random. LCG's worked well on computers that even a second-rate university could afford, and so the problem was solved, and life was good.

At some unknown point in here, presumably sometime in the 60's or 70's, someone seems to have invented Linear Feedback Shift Registers (LFSR's) as well. These made random-looking numbers and were really easy to implement in hardware compared to the LCG, which needed to do complicated things like multiply numbers. The random-looking numbers made by LFSR's were good enough for hardware people, so they started using LFSR's whenever they needed to and never looked back.

Anyway, by the late 60's people who knew how to use slide rules had
realized that using numbers that only *looked* random could really heck
up their math pretty bad, and one of the more common LCG implmentations,
RANDU, was actually about as bad as possible.  So, just using any old
LCG wasn't good enough, you had to use one made by someone with a PhD in
mathematics.  Donald Knuth shook his fist at the world and shouted "Hah!
I told you so!", published a book on how to do it Right that most people
didn't read, and then went back into his Fortress of Solitude to write
TeX.  Because it was created by IBM, RANDU's awfulness is now enshrined
forever in history documents like this one, and because the people
writing OS's and programming languages at the time weren't actually
doing much slide-rule stuff anymore and didn't actually *need* very good
random-looking numbers, everyone went back to using whatever old crap
RNG they were using anyway.  The problem was solved, or at least not
terribly problematic, and life was good.

Also, sometime in the 70's or 80's the arts of cryptography started leaking from classified government works into the real world. People started thinking about how much money they could make from scrambling satellite TV so that plebs with HAM radio licenses couldn't watch it, and these people started giving more money to people who had PhD's in mathematics to figure out how to make this work. It was quickly determined that neither LCG's nor LFSR's made numbers that were random-looking enough to really get in the way of someone who knew how to use a slide rule, and since Edith had long ago retired to a small beach house in New Jersey, they needed to figure out how to get computers to make better random-looking numbers. But making numbers look random enough that someone couldn't undo the process and get free pay-per-view was slow and involved lots of details that nobody else really cared about, so that topic went off on its own adventures and will not be further mentioned.

Things more or less trundled along this way until the late 90's, when suddenly computers were everywhere and there was a new generation of people who had grown up too late to know how to use slide rules, so they did all their math with computers. They were doing a LOT of math by now, and they looked around and realized that their random-looking numbers really weren't very random-looking at all, and this was actually something of a problem by now. So the Mersenne Twister got invented. It was pretty slow and used a lot of memory and made kinda mediocre random numbers, but it was way better than a bad LCG, and most importantly, it had a cool name. Most people didn't want to read Knuth's book and figure out how to make a non-bad LCG, so everyone started using the Mersenne Twister whenever possible. The problem was solved, and life was good.

This is where things stood until the early 2010's, when I finished my MS and started paying attention again. People suddenly realized it was possible to make random-looking numbers better than the Mersenne Twister using an algorithm called xorshift. Xorshift was fast, it made good pretty random-looking numbers, and it didn't need a whole 3 kilobytes of state just sitting around taking up space and causing comment among the neighbors at church. It did sometimes have problems with some of its numbers not looking random enough in a few select circumstances, but people were gun-shy about their randomness by now so a few people with PhD's in mathematics slowly and patiently spent years figuring out ways to work around these problems, leading to a whole confusing family of related things such as xoshiro, xoroshiro, xoroshiro+, xoroshiro*, and so on. Nobody else could really tell the difference between them, but everyone agreed they were better than Mersenne Twister, easier to implement, and the name was nearly as cool. Many papers were published, the problem was solved, and life was good.

However, at about the same time some bright young spark figured out that it actually wasn't too hard, if you read Knuth's book and thought real hard about what you were doing, to take the old LCG and hop it up on cocaine and moon juice. The result got called the Permuted Congruential Generator, or PCG. This quite miffed the people working on xorshift generators by being almost as small and fast, and producing random-looking numbers that satisfied even the people who had learned to use slide rules for fun in this latter age. It also used xor's and bit shifts, and that's xorshift's turf, dammit, it's right in the name! Since nobody had figured out any downsides to PCG's yet, everyone shrugged and said "might as well just go with that then", and that is where, as of 2019, the art currently stands. The problem is solved, and life is good.

---

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.2/

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of PCG generators. The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`aka- `Lcg64Xsh32`, officially known as- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`aka- `Lcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`aka- `Mcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

Both of these use 16 bytes of state and 128-bit seeds, and are considered value-stable (i.e. any change affecting the output given a fixed seed would be considered a breaking change to the crate).

| [Lcg128Xsl64](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg128Xsl64.html) | A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant). |
| [Lcg64Xsh32](https://docs.rs/struct.Lcg64Xsh32.html) | A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant). |
| [Mcg128Xsl64](https://docs.rs/struct.Mcg128Xsl64.html) | A PCG random number generator (XSL 128/64 (MCG) variant). |

| [Pcg32](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg32.html) |
 |
| [Pcg64](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg64.html) |
 |
| [Pcg64Mcg](https://docs.rs/type.Pcg64Mcg.html) | A friendly name for  |

# random_fast_rng - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/random-fast-rng/^0.1/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#random-fast-rng)Random-fast-rng

This crate provides a fast **non cryptographic** random number generator that implements the [ Random](https://docs.rs/trait.Random.html) trait.

Currently it’s implemented using the

`Pcg32` algorithm, that generates 32 bit of random data for every state change. the exact algorithm might change in the future, but the properties should stay the same (Blazing fast, non cryptographic, and minimal I/O) The crate is part of the

`random-rs` facade, and as such supports older rust compilers(currently 1.13+) and should have only thin amount of dependencies.This Random generator is good for testing uses, and use cases that require some non-determinism. it shouldn’t be used to generate keys/passwords.

By enabling the `std` feature this crate exposes a [ new()](https://docs.rs/struct.FastRng.html#method.new) function that uses

[to seed the RNG.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/time/struct.SystemTime.html)

`SystemTime::now()`It also exposes a

[function to give a persistent Rng that is seeded only once and is unique per thread (so there’s no need to worry about dropping and reinitializing the Rng)](https://docs.rs/fn.local_rng.html)

`local_rng()`## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub extern crate`- [random_trait](https://docs.rs/random-trait/0.1.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/random_trait/index.html);

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [FastRng](https://docs.rs/struct.FastRng.html)
- A FastRng struct implementing `Random``FastRng::seed()``std`feature is enabled call`FastRng::new()`
 For ergonomics and ease of usability the Rng is also provided as a global thread local variable using`FastRng::local_rng()`
- [Thread](https://docs.rs/struct.ThreadFastRng.html)- Fast - Rng
- A shim that points to the global `FastRng`instance. isn’t safe for multi-threading.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Random](https://docs.rs/trait.Random.html)
- This is the base trait of the crate. By implementing the required method on your random generator source
it will give you a long list of functions, the important of them is `Random::gen() -> T`which will produce a random value for every type which implements`GenerateRand`(you can implement this for your own types).

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [local_](https://docs.rs/fn.local_rng.html)- rng
- Returns a thread local instance which is seeded only once per thread (no need to worry about dropping and reinitializing)

# randomize - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/randomize/^3.0.0/

Simple and minimalist randomization.

NOT FOR CRYPTOGRAPHIC PURPOSES.

- Pick a generator, [PCG32](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG32.html)or[PCG64](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG64.html), depending on the output type you want.`PCG32`runs about 20% faster, so if you usually need 32 bits or less per use you might as well pick that.
- Seed your generator from wherever. However you wanna do it that your
platform supports. Major options would be the
`getrandom`[a hardware generator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/core_arch/x86_64/rdrand/fn._rdrand64_step.html)if available, the[CPU timing counter](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/core_arch/x86/rdtsc/fn._rdtsc.html)if there's no hardware generator, or even just a user input.
- The generators have a `state`and`inc`value. The`state`will change with each call, the`inc`is like a stream selection value that doesn't change when you use the generator. If you don't care about stream selection just pass your seed value to both arguments and it'll all "just work".
- Call [next_u32](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG32.html#method.next_u32)or[next_u64](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG64.html#method.next_u64)to get your numbers.
- You can use [RandRangeU32](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.RandRangeU32.html)for bounded integer randomization.

That's it, that's the whole lib. No generics, no traits, no breaking changes issued as patch releases, none of that.

Where generating `u32`s or `u64`s is not enough, you can wrap your generator
inside an [AnyPCG](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.AnyPCG.html) to generate non-floating-point integral values of any
size.

- Create a fixed-size generator, e.g. `let gen = PCG32::new(…);`
- Create an any-size generator from it: `let any = AnyPCG::new(gen);`
- Call the provided `next_*`functions for the corresponding integral types, such as[next_u16](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.AnyPCG.html#method.next_u16)to generate a`u16`while only taking 16 bits out of the random bit streams.

The more efficient use of generated bits comes at a barely noticeable cost
for [PCG32](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG32.html), and a bigger one for [PCG64](https://docs.rs/randomize/struct.PCG64.html). This only matters for batch
generation of big amounts of random data, though.

Unfortunately, there's many possible float distributions a person might want, so you'll have to call one of the float conversion functions yourself. I've included conversions for the five most commonly used floating point ranges.

| Range | 32-bit | 64-bit |
|---|---|---|
| `[0.0, 1.0)` | [f32_half_open_right](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f32_half_open_right.html) | [f64_half_open_right](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f64_half_open_right.html) |
| `(0.0, 1.0]` | [f32_half_open_left](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f32_half_open_left.html) | [f64_half_open_left](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f64_half_open_left.html) |
| `(0.0, 1.0)` | [f32_open](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f32_open.html) | [f64_open](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f64_open.html) |
| `[0.0, 1.0]` | [f32_closed](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f32_closed.html) | [f64_closed](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f64_closed.html) |
| `[-1.0, 1.0]` | [f32_closed_neg_pos](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f32_closed_neg_pos.html) | [f64_closed_neg_pos](https://docs.rs/randomize/formulas/fn.f64_closed_neg_pos.html) |

| `pub use ` |

| [formulas](https://docs.rs/formulas/index.html) | Various generator and conversion formulas. This module is a "junk drawer" of stuff. |

| [AnyPCG](https://docs.rs/struct.AnyPCG.html) | A wrapper around PCG types that generates any-size outputs without wasting random bits. |
| [PCG32](https://docs.rs/struct.PCG32.html) | A  |
| [PCG64](https://docs.rs/struct.PCG64.html) | A  |
| [RandRangeU32](https://docs.rs/struct.RandRangeU32.html) | An inclusive random range with a  |

# oorandom - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/oorandom/latest/target-redirect/oorandom/

## Expand description

A tiny, robust PRNG implementation.

More specifically, it implements a single GOOD PRNG algorithm,
which is currently a permuted congruential generator.  It has two
implementations, one that returns `u32` and one that returns
`u64`.  It also has functions that return floats or integer
ranges.  And that’s it.  What more do you need?

For more info on PCG generators, see http://www.pcg-random.org/

This was designed as a minimalist utility for video games. No promises are made about its quality, and if you use it for cryptography you will get what you deserve.

Works with `#![no_std]`, has no global state, no dependencies
apart from some in the unit tests, and is generally neato.

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

---

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# surtgis_algorithms - Rust

## Expand description

Geospatial analysis algorithms for SurtGis.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-algorithm-categories)Available Algorithm Categories

- **terrain**: Slope, aspect, hillshade, curvature, TPI, TRI, landform, TWI, SPI, STI, geomorphons, viewshed, SVF, openness, convergence, multiscale curvatures, feature-preserving smoothing, wind exposure, solar radiation, MRVBF/MRRTF, northness/eastness, DEV, multidirectional hillshade, shape index, curvedness, log transform, accumulation zones
- **hydrology**: Fill sinks, Priority-Flood, flow direction, flow accumulation, watershed, HAND, stream network
- **imagery**: Spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, NDRE, GNDVI, NGRDI, RECI, etc.), band math, reclassification
- **interpolation**: IDW, nearest neighbor, TIN
- **vector**: Buffer, simplify, spatial operations, clipping, measurements
- **morphology**: Erosion, dilation, opening, closing, gradient, top-hat, black-hat
- **statistics**: Focal statistics, zonal statistics, spatial autocorrelation

# tatara_net - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-net/0.2.122/tatara_net/

## Expand description

tatara-net: Cross-platform networking plane for the tatara cluster fabric.

The complete sandwich:

```
┌─ WASI (wasmtime) ──── Portable, sandboxed workloads ─────────┐
├─ Tatara Runtime ───── Convergence, scheduling, Raft ─────────┤
├─ eBPF (aya) ────────── Kernel hooks, pure Rust ──────────────┤
├─ WireGuard (mamorigami) ─ Encrypted mesh fabric ─────────────┤
└─ Hardware ──────────── Abstracted away ──────────────────────┘
```
On Linux: eBPF programs (XDP/TC/cgroup) for kernel-level networking. On macOS: userspace networking via tun-rs + smoltcp + hanabi proxy. Everywhere: WireGuard mesh via mamorigami for encrypted inter-node traffic.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [NetConfig](https://docs.rs/config/struct.NetConfig.html);
- `pub use traits::`- [NetworkPlane](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.NetworkPlane.html);
- `pub use`- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)::*;

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [config](https://docs.rs/config/index.html)
- Networking plane configuration.
- [convergence](https://docs.rs/convergence/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [mesh](https://docs.rs/mesh/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [observability](https://docs.rs/observability/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [platform](https://docs.rs/platform/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [policy](https://docs.rs/policy/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [routing](https://docs.rs/routing/index.html)
- Module stub — implementation in later phases.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)
- Core networking plane trait — platform-agnostic interface.
- [types](https://docs.rs/types/index.html)
- Core networking types for the tatara cluster fabric.

# tatara_wasm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-wasm/0.2.122/tatara_wasm/

## Expand description

`tatara-wasm` — multi-runtime WASI/WASM host for tatara guests.

Five runtimes, one trait, Cargo feature flags. Consumers pick the runtime per workload via the Lisp surface:

```
(defguest fast-fn   :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmtime …))
(defguest k8s-fn    :kind (:wasm :runtime :wasmedge …))
(defguest embed-fn  :kind (:wasm :runtime :wamr   :features (:aot #t :no-std #t)))
```
The runtime axis is first-class — all five are shipped with
production-grade implementations in Phase H.3 (wasmtime) and
H.4 (the rest). See `docs/declarative-guests.md`.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.1 stub.** The `WasmRuntime` enum + `WasmEngine` trait
land here now so `tatara-vm` can reference them. Runtime bodies
are empty until H.3/H.4.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use engine::`- [engine_for](https://docs.rs/engine/fn.engine_for.html);
- `pub use engine::`- [WasmBoot](https://docs.rs/engine/struct.WasmBoot.html);
- `pub use engine::`- [WasmEngine](https://docs.rs/engine/trait.WasmEngine.html);
- `pub use engine::`- [WasmEngineError](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.WasmEngineError.html);
- `pub use engine::`- [WasmHandle](https://docs.rs/engine/struct.WasmHandle.html);
- `pub use engine::`- [WasmModuleSource](https://docs.rs/engine/enum.WasmModuleSource.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [engine](https://docs.rs/engine/index.html)
- The `WasmEngine`trait — polymorphic over runtime.
- [wasmtime_](https://docs.rs/wasmtime_impl/index.html)- impl
- wasmtime backend. Compiled in with `runtime-wasmtime`.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/struct.WasmFeatures.html)- Features
- Feature toggles the runtime must honor.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Wasi](https://docs.rs/enum.WasiPreview.html)- Preview
- WASI version the guest expects.
- [Wasm](https://docs.rs/enum.WasmRuntime.html)- Runtime
- Which WASM runtime hosts this guest.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS
- Phase H.1 placeholder. Replaced in H.3 / H.4 with the real engine trait wired to each runtime.

# surtgis_colormap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/surtgis-colormap/0.17.0/surtgis_colormap/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#surtgis-colormap)SurtGis Colormap

Color mapping and raster-to-RGBA rendering for SurtGis.

Provides 8 predefined color schemes ported from the web demo, plus a generic
multi-stop interpolation engine. The main entry point is [ raster_to_rgba](https://docs.rs/fn.raster_to_rgba.html)
which converts a

`Raster<T>` into an RGBA pixel buffer suitable for GPU textures.[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/struct.ColorStop.html)- Stop
- A color stop: position in [0, 1] mapped to an RGB color.
- [Colormap](https://docs.rs/struct.ColormapParams.html)- Params
- Parameters for colormap rendering.
- [Rgb](https://docs.rs/struct.Rgb.html)
- RGB color as (r, g, b) with values in 0..=255.
- [Rgba](https://docs.rs/struct.RgbaImage.html)- Image
- Row-major 8-bit RGBA pixel buffer.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Color](https://docs.rs/enum.ColorScheme.html)- Scheme
- Available color schemes.
- [Encode](https://docs.rs/enum.EncodeError.html)- Error
- Errors produced when building or encoding an `RgbaImage`

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [auto_](https://docs.rs/fn.auto_params.html)- params
- Auto-detect min/max from a raster, returning `ColormapParams`ready to use.
- [evaluate](https://docs.rs/fn.evaluate.html)
- Evaluate a color scheme at normalized position `t`∈ [0, 1].
- [raster_](https://docs.rs/fn.raster_to_rgba.html)- to_ - rgba
- Convert a raster to an RGBA pixel buffer.
- [rgba_](https://docs.rs/fn.rgba_to_png_bytes.html)- to_ - png_ - bytes
- Encode an arbitrary RGBA byte buffer as PNG. Native target only.
- [save_](https://docs.rs/fn.save_png.html)- png
- Write an RGBA buffer to `path`as a PNG. Native target only.

# sequoia_openpgp - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sequoia-openpgp/2.4.0/sequoia_openpgp/

## Expand description

OpenPGP data types and associated machinery.

This crate aims to provide a complete implementation of OpenPGP as
defined by [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) as well as the deprecated OpenPGP as defined
by [RFC 4880](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4880).  OpenPGP is a standard by the IETF.  It was derived
from the PGP software, which was created by Phil Zimmermann in
1991.

This crate also includes support for unbuffered message processing.

A few features that the OpenPGP community considers to be deprecated (e.g., version 3 compatibility) have been left out. We have also updated some OpenPGP defaults to avoid foot guns (e.g., we selected modern algorithm defaults). If some functionality is missing, please file a bug report.

A non-goal of this crate is support for any sort of high-level,
bolted-on functionality.  For instance, [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) does not define
trust models, such as the web of trust, direct trust, or TOFU.
Neither does this crate.  [RFC 9580](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9580.html) does provide some mechanisms
for creating trust models (specifically, UserID certifications),
and this crate does expose those mechanisms.

We also try hard to avoid dictating how OpenPGP should be used. This doesn’t mean that we don’t have opinions about how OpenPGP should be used in a number of common scenarios (for instance, message validation). But, in this crate, we refrain from expressing those opinions; we will expose an opinionated, high-level interface in the future. In order to figure out the most appropriate high-level interfaces, we look at existing users. If you are using Sequoia, please get in contact so that we can learn from your use cases, discuss your opinions, and develop a high-level interface based on these experiences in the future.

Despite —or maybe because of— its unopinionated nature we found it easy to develop opinionated OpenPGP software based on Sequoia.

[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-features)Experimental Features

This crate may implement extensions where the standardization effort is still ongoing. These experimental features are marked as such in the documentation. We invite you to experiment with them, but please do expect the semantics and possibly even the wire format to evolve.

# tatara_hvf - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-hvf/0.2.122/tatara_hvf/

## Expand description

`tatara-hvf` — Apple Hypervisor.framework backend for tatara guests.

The **bare-metal** VM engine. Direct `hv_vm_*` / `hv_vcpu_*` calls
via the `applevisor` safe-wrapper crate, own virtio device backends
(landing H.2.2), raw vCPU loop with MMIO callbacks.

[§](https://docs.rs#layering)Layering

```
  tatara-hvf (this crate)
      │  uses
      ▼
  applevisor (safe wrapper — Quarkslab)
      │  links
      ▼
  Hypervisor.framework  (aarch64-darwin only)
```
[§](https://docs.rs#cargo--build)Cargo / build

The `applevisor` dep is target-gated to `aarch64-darwin`. On any
other target, the crate compiles but `HvfEngine::new()` returns
`HvfError::UnsupportedPlatform`. This keeps `cargo check --workspace` clean on Linux CI while the real engine is only
exercised on M-series Macs.

[§](https://docs.rs#entitlements)Entitlements

Running any HVF binary requires the `com.apple.security.hypervisor`
entitlement. For `cargo test`, either codesign the test binary
with an entitlements plist or run tests as root. Currently:

```
codesign --entitlements entitlements.plist --sign - \
  target/debug/deps/tatara_hvf-*
```
A follow-up CI helper crate will encapsulate this; for now the
`vm_create_is_supported` test is `#[ignore]` by default so `cargo test` doesn’t fail when entitlements aren’t set.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use stub::`- [HvfEngine](https://docs.rs/stub/struct.HvfEngine.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [stub](https://docs.rs/stub/index.html)
- Non-aarch64-darwin stub. HVF doesn’t exist on Linux / Intel Mac, so
`HvfEngine::new()`returns a typed error. The struct still exists so downstream crates compile.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Guest](https://docs.rs/struct.GuestRegion.html)- Region
- A guest memory region mapped into the VM’s physical address space.
- [Permissions](https://docs.rs/struct.Permissions.html)
- Page permissions for a mapped region.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [HvfError](https://docs.rs/enum.HvfError.html)
- Errors from the HVF backend.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [CRATE_](https://docs.rs/constant.CRATE_STATUS.html)- STATUS
- Phase marker.

# tatara_build_remote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tatara-build-remote/0.2.122/tatara_build_remote/

## Expand description

`tatara-build-remote` — layered Nix build transport for tatara guests.

Takes a `BuildRef` (flake + attr, raw Nix expression, store path, or
OCI image) and resolves it to a concrete `StorePath` using a
priority-ordered chain of transports. **First match wins.** Default
chain:

- **Attic cache**— pulls from a shared Attic instance (e.g.- `quero.lol`). Fastest path when the artifact is already cached.
- **ssh-ng remote builder**— submits to a remote Nix builder over- `ssh-ng://`. Used when Attic misses and the local machine can’t or shouldn’t build (cross-arch, resource constrained, etc.).
- **Local**—- `nix build`on the host. Last resort.

Any transport declared absent in the spec is skipped. If all declared
transports fail, `BuildError::AllTransportsFailed` bubbles up and
hospedeiro refuses to boot the guest — we fail closed.

[§](https://docs.rs#status)Status

**Phase H.5 landed.** `AtticTransport`, `SshRemoteTransport`, and
`LocalTransport` all ship in `transports.rs`.
`BuildTransportChain::to_layered()` composes them into a priority-
ordered `LayeredTransport` driven by `(defguest …)`’s `:build-on`
keyword.

[§](https://docs.rs#why-layered-not-single-target)Why layered, not single-target

The fleet at `quero.lol` has a shared Attic cache *and* an ssh-ng
builder pool. Cache hits are free; builds are expensive. Layering
lets the common case (pleme-io team members pulling pre-built
artifacts) skip the slow path entirely. Keys + SSH config come from
the cid node’s `pangea-builder.nix` — no new auth plumbing.

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use transports::`- [AtticTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.AtticTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [LocalTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.LocalTransport.html);
- `pub use transports::`- [SshRemoteTransport](https://docs.rs/transports/struct.SshRemoteTransport.html);

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- Concrete `BuildTransport`implementations.

- Declarative transport chain. A `None`field means “don’t try this transport”.
- [Layered](https://docs.rs/struct.LayeredTransport.html)- Transport
- Layered transport — tries each child in order, returns the first success.
- [Store](https://docs.rs/struct.StorePath.html)- Path
- A Nix store path — content-addressed handle.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Build](https://docs.rs/enum.BuildRef.html)- Ref
- A reference to something that becomes a Nix store path.

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

# oorandom 11.1.5 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/oorandom/11.1.5

# oorandom

# What is this?

`oorandom` is a minimalistic pseudorandom number generator in Rust.  For
those times when the `rand` crate is just too big and you want something
a bit dumber.

More specifically, it implements ONE prng, which is currently a permuted
congruential generator (PCG).  It may change if something better comes
along, but that seems unlikely and will probably be a major version
bump.  It will give you `u32` or `u64`, and signed or floating-point
equivalents.  It is also `#[no_std]`.  Anything else is gravy.

Thanks to Lokathor for making
[ randomize](https://github.com/Lokathor/randomize), which inspired me
to do my own equivalent.

The name comes from my attempts to find a good way to pronounce
`/dev/urandom`.

Please direct questions, discussions and bugs to the [issue
tracker](https://todo.sr.ht/~icefox/oorandom).

# Why use `oorandom` instead of...

- `rand`--- `oorandom`is simpler and has zero choices you need to make. It also compiles in 1/10th the time and has a stable API.
- `getrandom`-- They solve different problems;- `getrandom`gives you whatever secure randomness the OS decides to give you, not a deterministic and seedable PRNG. It's generally a good idea to use- `getrandom`to seed this RNG though.
- `randomize`--- `randomize`used to be more complicated, but- `randomize`3.x is quite similar to- `oorandom`in functionality and design. Go for it.
- `rand_pcg`and- `rand_core`-- Yes you can take- `rand`apart into its pieces and use those individually, if you want to abandon having an all-in-one solution, still deal with the lack of stability in- `rand_core`and actually figure out which pieces you need. It works just fine. Seems more complicated than it needs to be though.
- `nanorand`--- `nanorand`uses the- [WyRand](https://github.com/wangyi-fudan/wyhash)PRNG algorithm, which is supposedly faster than PCG and at least as good quality. I haven't verified these claims, and I don't know of any- *really*thorough 3rd party investigation into them, though it apparently passes- [Dr. Lemire's tests](https://github.com/lemire/testingRNG). So for now I personally consider WyRand to be in the "trust but verify" level of quality. It's probably fine. Check back in 2027.
- `fastrand`-- Looks fine, uses the same algorithm as- `oorandom`. Made by the same people as the- `smol`async runtime, which may be good or bad for you. Does slightly more than- `oorandom`does, which may be good or bad for you. Use it if you like it.

# This is not...

This is not cryptographically secure, and if you use it for crypto you
will get what you deserve.  You are also in charge of choosing a useful
seed; the `getrandom` crate might be useful for that.

This is also not optimized to be stupidly fast, but is basically just
as fast as `rustc` feels like making it.  This means it is safe and robust
and portable and involves absolutely zero clever tricks.

# Usage

```
use oorandom;
```
If you want a nondeterministic seed, I recommend using the `getrandom` crate to produce one.

# License

MIT

# A brief history of random numbers

The usefulness of random numbers has been known for a long, long time to people who also knew how to use slide rules. If you wanted to do some math without the bother of coming up with all that pesky input data from the real world, you might as well just use any ol' random numbers, as long as there weren't any patterns in them to heck up the patterns you were trying to look at. So in the first half of the 20th century you had little old ladies named Edith spinning roulette wheels or pulling bingo balls out of baskets and writing the results down, which got assembled into giant tomes and published so that engineering schools could buy them and have giant tomes sitting on their shelves. Anyone who wanted some meaningless numbers could pull the tome down, flip it open to a presumably-random page, and there were all the random numbers anyone could want. The problem was solved, and life was good.

In late 1940's computers were invented, but they were far too big and
expensive to be put on the task of *intentionally* generating
nonsense, and things carried on as before.  If you needed random
numbers in a computer program, you just got a pretty young lady named
Mary to transcribe part of the book to punch cards for you.

Around the early 1960's computers got fast enough that Edith and Mary couldn't keep up with them, so they got downsized and replaced with more computers. To do this people came up with Linear Congruential Generators (LCG's), which could generate lots of numbers numbers that weren't really random, but sure looked random. LCG's worked well on computers that even a second-rate university could afford, and so the problem was solved, and life was good.

At some unknown point in here, presumably sometime in the 60's or 70's, someone seems to have invented Linear Feedback Shift Registers (LFSR's) as well. These made random-looking numbers and were really easy to implement in hardware compared to the LCG, which needed to do complicated things like multiply numbers. The random-looking numbers made by LFSR's were good enough for hardware people, so they started using LFSR's whenever they needed to and never looked back.

Anyway, by the late 60's people who knew how to use slide rules had
realized that using numbers that only *looked* random could really heck
up their math pretty bad, and one of the more common LCG implmentations,
RANDU, was actually about as bad as possible.  So, just using any old
LCG wasn't good enough, you had to use one made by someone with a PhD in
mathematics.  Donald Knuth shook his fist at the world and shouted "Hah!
I told you so!", published a book on how to do it Right that most people
didn't read, and then went back into his Fortress of Solitude to write
TeX.  Because it was created by IBM, RANDU's awfulness is now enshrined
forever in history documents like this one, and because the people
writing OS's and programming languages at the time weren't actually
doing much slide-rule stuff anymore and didn't actually *need* very good
random-looking numbers, everyone went back to using whatever old crap
RNG they were using anyway.  The problem was solved, or at least not
terribly problematic, and life was good.

Also, sometime in the 70's or 80's the arts of cryptography started leaking from classified government works into the real world. People started thinking about how much money they could make from scrambling satellite TV so that plebs with HAM radio licenses couldn't watch it, and these people started giving more money to people who had PhD's in mathematics to figure out how to make this work. It was quickly determined that neither LCG's nor LFSR's made numbers that were random-looking enough to really get in the way of someone who knew how to use a slide rule, and since Edith had long ago retired to a small beach house in New Jersey, they needed to figure out how to get computers to make better random-looking numbers. But making numbers look random enough that someone couldn't undo the process and get free pay-per-view was slow and involved lots of details that nobody else really cared about, so that topic went off on its own adventures and will not be further mentioned.

Things more or less trundled along this way until the late 90's, when suddenly computers were everywhere and there was a new generation of people who had grown up too late to know how to use slide rules, so they did all their math with computers. They were doing a LOT of math by now, and they looked around and realized that their random-looking numbers really weren't very random-looking at all, and this was actually something of a problem by now. So the Mersenne Twister got invented. It was pretty slow and used a lot of memory and made kinda mediocre random numbers, but it was way better than a bad LCG, and most importantly, it had a cool name. Most people didn't want to read Knuth's book and figure out how to make a non-bad LCG, so everyone started using the Mersenne Twister whenever possible. The problem was solved, and life was good.

This is where things stood until the early 2010's, when I finished my MS and started paying attention again. People suddenly realized it was possible to make random-looking numbers better than the Mersenne Twister using an algorithm called xorshift. Xorshift was fast, it made good pretty random-looking numbers, and it didn't need a whole 3 kilobytes of state just sitting around taking up space and causing comment among the neighbors at church. It did sometimes have problems with some of its numbers not looking random enough in a few select circumstances, but people were gun-shy about their randomness by now so a few people with PhD's in mathematics slowly and patiently spent years figuring out ways to work around these problems, leading to a whole confusing family of related things such as xoshiro, xoroshiro, xoroshiro+, xoroshiro*, and so on. Nobody else could really tell the difference between them, but everyone agreed they were better than Mersenne Twister, easier to implement, and the name was nearly as cool. Many papers were published, the problem was solved, and life was good.

However, at about the same time some bright young spark figured out that it actually wasn't too hard, if you read Knuth's book and thought real hard about what you were doing, to take the old LCG and hop it up on cocaine and moon juice. The result got called the Permuted Congruential Generator, or PCG. This quite miffed the people working on xorshift generators by being almost as small and fast, and producing random-looking numbers that satisfied even the people who had learned to use slide rules for fun in this latter age. It also used xor's and bit shifts, and that's xorshift's turf, dammit, it's right in the name! Since nobody had figured out any downsides to PCG's yet, everyone shrugged and said "might as well just go with that then", and that is where, as of 2019, the art currently stands. The problem is solved, and life is good.

---

                    oorandom 11.1.5

# oorandom - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/oorandom/11.1.5/target-redirect/oorandom/

## Expand description

A tiny, robust PRNG implementation.

More specifically, it implements a single GOOD PRNG algorithm,
which is currently a permuted congruential generator.  It has two
implementations, one that returns `u32` and one that returns
`u64`.  It also has functions that return floats or integer
ranges.  And that’s it.  What more do you need?

For more info on PCG generators, see http://www.pcg-random.org/

This was designed as a minimalist utility for video games. No promises are made about its quality, and if you use it for cryptography you will get what you deserve.

Works with `#![no_std]`, has no global state, no dependencies
apart from some in the unit tests, and is generally neato.

[25](https://docs.rs#25)/// A PRNG producing a 32-bit output.
[26](https://docs.rs#26)///
[27](https://docs.rs#27)/// The current implementation is `PCG-XSH-RR`.
[28](https://docs.rs#28)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
[29](https://docs.rs#29)pub struct Rand32 {
[30](https://docs.rs#30)    state: u64,
[31](https://docs.rs#31)    inc: u64,
[32](https://docs.rs#32)}
[33](https://docs.rs#33)
[34](https://docs.rs#34)impl Rand32 {
[35](https://docs.rs#35)    /// The default value for `increment`.
[36](https://docs.rs#36)    /// This is basically arbitrary, it comes from the
[37](https://docs.rs#37)    /// PCG reference C implementation:
[38](https://docs.rs#38)    /// https://github.com/imneme/pcg-c/blob/master/include/pcg_variants.h#L284
[39](https://docs.rs#39)    pub const DEFAULT_INC: u64 = 1442695040888963407;
[40](https://docs.rs#40)
[41](https://docs.rs#41)    /// This is the number that you have to Really Get Right.
[42](https://docs.rs#42)    ///
[43](https://docs.rs#43)    /// The value used here is from the PCG C implementation:
[44](https://docs.rs#44)    /// https://github.com/imneme/pcg-c/blob/master/include/pcg_variants.h#L278
[45](https://docs.rs#45)    pub(crate) const MULTIPLIER: u64 = 6364136223846793005;
[46](https://docs.rs#46)
[47](https://docs.rs#47)    /// Creates a new PRNG with the given seed and a default increment.
[48](https://docs.rs#48)    pub fn new(seed: u64) -> Self {
[49](https://docs.rs#49)        Self::new_inc(seed, Self::DEFAULT_INC)
[50](https://docs.rs#50)    }
[51](https://docs.rs#51)
[52](https://docs.rs#52)    /// Creates a new PRNG.  The two inputs, `seed` and `increment`,
[53](https://docs.rs#53)    /// determine what you get; `increment` basically selects which
[54](https://docs.rs#54)    /// sequence of all those possible the PRNG will produce, and the
[55](https://docs.rs#55)    /// `seed` selects where in that sequence you start.
[56](https://docs.rs#56)    ///
[57](https://docs.rs#57)    /// Both are arbitrary; increment must be an odd number but this
[58](https://docs.rs#58)    /// handles that for you
[59](https://docs.rs#59)    pub fn new_inc(seed: u64, increment: u64) -> Self {
[60](https://docs.rs#60)        let mut rng = Self {
[61](https://docs.rs#61)            state: 0,
[62](https://docs.rs#62)            inc: increment.wrapping_shl(1) | 1,
[63](https://docs.rs#63)        };
[64](https://docs.rs#64)        // This initialization song-and-dance is a little odd,
[65](https://docs.rs#65)        // but seems to be just how things go.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)        let _ = rng.rand_u32();
[67](https://docs.rs#67)        rng.state = rng.state.wrapping_add(seed);
[68](https://docs.rs#68)        let _ = rng.rand_u32();
[69](https://docs.rs#69)        rng
[70](https://docs.rs#70)    }
[71](https://docs.rs#71)
[72](https://docs.rs#72)    /// Returns the internal state of the PRNG.  This allows
[73](https://docs.rs#73)    /// you to save a PRNG and create a new one that will resume
[74](https://docs.rs#74)    /// from the same spot in the sequence.
[75](https://docs.rs#75)    pub fn state(&self) -> (u64, u64) {
[76](https://docs.rs#76)        (self.state, self.inc)
[77](https://docs.rs#77)    }
[78](https://docs.rs#78)
[79](https://docs.rs#79)    /// Creates a new PRNG from a saved state from `Rand32::state()`.
[80](https://docs.rs#80)    /// This is NOT quite the same as `new_inc()` because `new_inc()` does
[81](https://docs.rs#81)    /// a little extra setup work to initialize the state.
[82](https://docs.rs#82)    pub fn from_state(state: (u64, u64)) -> Self {
[83](https://docs.rs#83)        let (state, inc) = state;
[84](https://docs.rs#84)        Self { state, inc }
[85](https://docs.rs#85)    }
[86](https://docs.rs#86)
[87](https://docs.rs#87)    /// Produces a random `u32` in the range `[0, u32::MAX]`.
[88](https://docs.rs#88)    pub fn rand_u32(&mut self) -> u32 {
[89](https://docs.rs#89)        let oldstate: u64 = self.state;
[90](https://docs.rs#90)        self.state = oldstate
[91](https://docs.rs#91)            .wrapping_mul(Self::MULTIPLIER)
[92](https://docs.rs#92)            .wrapping_add(self.inc);
[93](https://docs.rs#93)        let xorshifted: u32 = (((oldstate >> 18) ^ oldstate) >> 27) as u32;
[94](https://docs.rs#94)        let rot: u32 = (oldstate >> 59) as u32;
[95](https://docs.rs#95)        xorshifted.rotate_right(rot)
[96](https://docs.rs#96)    }
[97](https://docs.rs#97)
[98](https://docs.rs#98)    /// Produces a random `i32` in the range `[i32::MIN, i32::MAX]`.
[99](https://docs.rs#99)    pub fn rand_i32(&mut self) -> i32 {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)        self.rand_u32() as i32
[101](https://docs.rs#101)    }
[102](https://docs.rs#102)
[103](https://docs.rs#103)    /// Produces a random `f32` in the range `[0.0, 1.0)`.
[104](https://docs.rs#104)    pub fn rand_float(&mut self) -> f32 {
[105](https://docs.rs#105)        // This impl was taken more or less from `rand`, see
[106](https://docs.rs#106)        // <https://docs.rs/rand/0.7.0/src/rand/distributions/float.rs.html#104-117>
[107](https://docs.rs#107)        // Note that we use f32::MANTISSA_DIGITS = 24, where that impl passes the
[108](https://docs.rs#108)        // number as an input to the macro and uses 23 so needs a +1.
[109](https://docs.rs#109)        // See https://todo.sr.ht/~icefox/oorandom/9
[110](https://docs.rs#110)        // There MAY be better ways to do this, see:
[111](https://docs.rs#111)        // https://mumble.net/~campbell/2014/04/28/uniform-random-float
[112](https://docs.rs#112)        // https://mumble.net/~campbell/2014/04/28/random_real.c
[113](https://docs.rs#113)        // https://github.com/Lokathor/randomize/issues/34
[114](https://docs.rs#114)        const TOTAL_BITS: u32 = 32;
[115](https://docs.rs#115)        const PRECISION: u32 = core::f32::MANTISSA_DIGITS;
[116](https://docs.rs#116)        const MANTISSA_SCALE: f32 = 1.0 / ((1u32 << PRECISION) as f32);
[117](https://docs.rs#117)        let mut u = self.rand_u32();
[118](https://docs.rs#118)        u >>= TOTAL_BITS - PRECISION;
[119](https://docs.rs#119)        u as f32 * MANTISSA_SCALE
[120](https://docs.rs#120)    }
[121](https://docs.rs#121)
[122](https://docs.rs#122)    /// Produces a random within the given bounds.  Like any `Range`,
[123](https://docs.rs#123)    /// it includes the lower bound and excludes the upper one.
[124](https://docs.rs#124)    ///
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    /// This should be faster than `Self::rand() % end + start`, but the
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    /// real advantage is it's more convenient.  Requires that
[127](https://docs.rs#127)    /// `range.end <= range.start`.
[128](https://docs.rs#128)    pub fn rand_range(&mut self, range: Range<u32>) -> u32 {
[129](https://docs.rs#129)        // This is harder to do well than it looks, it seems.  I don't
[130](https://docs.rs#130)        // trust Lokathor's implementation 'cause I don't understand
[131](https://docs.rs#131)        // it, so I went to numpy's, which points me to "Lemire's
[132](https://docs.rs#132)        // rejection algorithm": http://arxiv.org/abs/1805.10941
[133](https://docs.rs#133)        //
[134](https://docs.rs#134)        // Algorithms 3, 4 and 5 in that paper all seem fine modulo
[135](https://docs.rs#135)        // minor performance differences, so this is algorithm 5.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        // It uses numpy's implementation, `buffered_bounded_lemire_uint32()`
[137](https://docs.rs#137)
[138](https://docs.rs#138)        debug_assert!(range.start < range.end);
[139](https://docs.rs#139)        let range_starting_from_zero = 0..(range.end - range.start);
[140](https://docs.rs#140)
[141](https://docs.rs#141)        let s: u32 = range_starting_from_zero.end;
[142](https://docs.rs#142)        let mut m: u64 = u64::from(self.rand_u32()) * u64::from(s);
[143](https://docs.rs#143)        let mut leftover: u32 = (m & 0xFFFF_FFFF) as u32;
[144](https://docs.rs#144)
[145](https://docs.rs#145)        if leftover < s {
[146](https://docs.rs#146)            // TODO: verify the wrapping_neg() here
[147](https://docs.rs#147)            let threshold: u32 = s.wrapping_neg() % s;
[148](https://docs.rs#148)            while leftover < threshold {
[149](https://docs.rs#149)                m = u64::from(self.rand_u32()).wrapping_mul(u64::from(s));
[150](https://docs.rs#150)                leftover = (m & 0xFFFF_FFFF) as u32;
[151](https://docs.rs#151)            }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)        }
[153](https://docs.rs#153)        (m >> 32) as u32 + range.start
[154](https://docs.rs#154)    }
[155](https://docs.rs#155)}
[156](https://docs.rs#156)
[157](https://docs.rs#157)/// A PRNG producing a 64-bit output.
[158](https://docs.rs#158)///
[159](https://docs.rs#159)/// The current implementation is `PCG-XSH-RR`.
[160](https://docs.rs#160)// BUGGO: The recommended algorithm is PCG-XSL-RR?
[161](https://docs.rs#161)// See https://github.com/imneme/pcg-c/blob/master/include/pcg_variants.h#L2405
[162](https://docs.rs#162)// Not sure if it matters?
[163](https://docs.rs#163)#[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, PartialEq, Eq)]
[164](https://docs.rs#164)pub struct Rand64 {
[165](https://docs.rs#165)    state: u128,
[166](https://docs.rs#166)    inc: u128,
[167](https://docs.rs#167)}
[168](https://docs.rs#168)
[169](https://docs.rs#169)impl Rand64 {
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// The default value for `increment`.
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    ///
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// The value used here is from the PCG default C implementation: http://www.pcg-random.org/download.html
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    pub const DEFAULT_INC: u128 = 0x2FE0E169_FFBD06E3_5BC307BD_4D2F814F;
[174](https://docs.rs#174)
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// This is the number that you have to Really Get Right.
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    ///
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// The value used here is from the PCG C implementation:
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// https://github.com/imneme/pcg-c/blob/master/include/pcg_variants.h#L288
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    pub(crate) const MULTIPLIER: u128 = 47026247687942121848144207491837523525;
[180](https://docs.rs#180)
[181](https://docs.rs#181)    /// Creates a new PRNG with the given seed and a default increment.
[182](https://docs.rs#182)    pub fn new(seed: u128) -> Self {
[183](https://docs.rs#183)        Self::new_inc(seed, Self::DEFAULT_INC)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)    }
[185](https://docs.rs#185)
[186](https://docs.rs#186)    /// Same as `Rand32::new_inc()`
[187](https://docs.rs#187)    pub fn new_inc(seed: u128, increment: u128) -> Self {
[188](https://docs.rs#188)        let mut rng = Self {
[189](https://docs.rs#189)            state: 0,
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            inc: increment.wrapping_shl(1) | 1,
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        };
[192](https://docs.rs#192)        let _ = rng.rand_u64();
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        rng.state = rng.state.wrapping_add(seed);
[194](https://docs.rs#194)        let _ = rng.rand_u64();
[195](https://docs.rs#195)        rng
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    }
[197](https://docs.rs#197)
[198](https://docs.rs#198)    /// Returns the internal state of the PRNG.  This allows
[199](https://docs.rs#199)    /// you to save a PRNG and create a new one that will resume
[200](https://docs.rs#200)    /// from the same spot in the sequence.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)    pub fn state(&self) -> (u128, u128) {
[202](https://docs.rs#202)        (self.state, self.inc)
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    }
[204](https://docs.rs#204)
[205](https://docs.rs#205)    /// Creates a new PRNG from a saved state from `Rand32::state()`.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)    /// This is NOT quite the same as `new_inc()` because `new_inc()` does
[207](https://docs.rs#207)    /// a little extra setup work to initialize the state.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    pub fn from_state(state: (u128, u128)) -> Self {
[209](https://docs.rs#209)        let (state, inc) = state;
[210](https://docs.rs#210)        Self { state, inc }
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    }
[212](https://docs.rs#212)
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// Produces a random `u64` in the range`[0, u64::MAX]`.
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    pub fn rand_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
[215](https://docs.rs#215)        let oldstate: u128 = self.state;
[216](https://docs.rs#216)        self.state = oldstate
[217](https://docs.rs#217)            .wrapping_mul(Self::MULTIPLIER)
[218](https://docs.rs#218)            .wrapping_add(self.inc);
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        let xorshifted: u64 = (((oldstate >> 29) ^ oldstate) >> 58) as u64;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)        let rot: u32 = (oldstate >> 122) as u32;
[221](https://docs.rs#221)        xorshifted.rotate_right(rot)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    }
[223](https://docs.rs#223)
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    /// Produces a random `i64` in the range `[i64::MIN, i64::MAX]`.
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    pub fn rand_i64(&mut self) -> i64 {
[226](https://docs.rs#226)        self.rand_u64() as i64
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    }
[228](https://docs.rs#228)
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// Produces a random `f64` in the range `[0.0, 1.0)`.
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    pub fn rand_float(&mut self) -> f64 {
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        const TOTAL_BITS: u32 = 64;
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        const PRECISION: u32 = core::f64::MANTISSA_DIGITS;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        const MANTISSA_SCALE: f64 = 1.0 / ((1u64 << PRECISION) as f64);
[234](https://docs.rs#234)        let mut u = self.rand_u64();
[235](https://docs.rs#235)        u >>= TOTAL_BITS - PRECISION;
[236](https://docs.rs#236)        u as f64 * MANTISSA_SCALE
[237](https://docs.rs#237)    }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    /// Produces a random within the given bounds.  Like any `Range`,
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    /// it includes the lower bound and excludes the upper one.
[241](https://docs.rs#241)    ///
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    /// This should be faster than `Self::rand() % end + start`, but the
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    /// real advantage is it's more convenient.  Requires that
[244](https://docs.rs#244)    /// `range.end <= range.start`.
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    pub fn rand_range(&mut self, range: Range<u64>) -> u64 {
[246](https://docs.rs#246)        // Same as `Rand32::rand_range()`
[247](https://docs.rs#247)        debug_assert!(range.start < range.end);
[248](https://docs.rs#248)        let range_starting_from_zero = 0..(range.end - range.start);
[249](https://docs.rs#249)
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        let s: u64 = range_starting_from_zero.end;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)        let mut m: u128 = u128::from(self.rand_u64()) * u128::from(s);
[252](https://docs.rs#252)        let mut leftover: u64 = (m & 0xFFFFFFFF_FFFFFFFF) as u64;
[253](https://docs.rs#253)
[254](https://docs.rs#254)        if leftover < s {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)            // TODO: Verify the wrapping_negate() here
[256](https://docs.rs#256)            let threshold: u64 = s.wrapping_neg() % s;
[257](https://docs.rs#257)            while leftover < threshold {
[258](https://docs.rs#258)                m = u128::from(self.rand_u64()) * u128::from(s);
[259](https://docs.rs#259)                leftover = (m & 0xFFFFFFFF_FFFFFFFF) as u64;
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            }
[261](https://docs.rs#261)        }
[262](https://docs.rs#262)        (m.wrapping_shr(64)) as u64 + range.start
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    }
[264](https://docs.rs#264)}

[271](https://docs.rs#271)    #[test]
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    fn test_rand32_vs_randomize() {
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        // Generate some random numbers and validate them against
[274](https://docs.rs#274)        // a known-good generator.
[275](https://docs.rs#275)        {
[276](https://docs.rs#276)            let seed = 54321;
[277](https://docs.rs#277)            let mut r1 = Rand32::new(seed);
[278](https://docs.rs#278)            let mut r2 = PCG32::seed(seed, Rand32::DEFAULT_INC);
[279](https://docs.rs#279)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_u32(), r2.next_u32());
[281](https://docs.rs#281)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_i32(), r2.next_u32() as i32);
[282](https://docs.rs#282)            }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        }
[284](https://docs.rs#284)
[285](https://docs.rs#285)        {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)            let seed = 3141592653;
[287](https://docs.rs#287)            let inc = 0xDEADBEEF;
[288](https://docs.rs#288)            let mut r1 = Rand32::new_inc(seed, inc);
[289](https://docs.rs#289)            let mut r2 = PCG32::seed(seed, inc);
[290](https://docs.rs#290)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[291](https://docs.rs#291)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_u32(), r2.next_u32());
[292](https://docs.rs#292)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_i32(), r2.next_u32() as i32);
[293](https://docs.rs#293)            }
[294](https://docs.rs#294)        }
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    }

[297](https://docs.rs#297)    #[test]
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    fn test_rand64_vs_randomize() {
[299](https://docs.rs#299)        // Generate some random numbers and validate them against
[300](https://docs.rs#300)        // a known-good generator.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)        {
[302](https://docs.rs#302)            let seed = 54321;
[303](https://docs.rs#303)            let mut r1 = Rand64::new(seed);
[304](https://docs.rs#304)            let mut r2 = PCG64::seed(seed, Rand64::DEFAULT_INC);
[305](https://docs.rs#305)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[306](https://docs.rs#306)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_u64(), r2.next_u64());
[307](https://docs.rs#307)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_i64(), r2.next_u64() as i64);
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            }
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        }
[310](https://docs.rs#310)
[311](https://docs.rs#311)        {
[312](https://docs.rs#312)            let seed = 3141592653;
[313](https://docs.rs#313)            let inc = 0xDEADBEEF;
[314](https://docs.rs#314)            let mut r1 = Rand64::new_inc(seed, inc);
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            let mut r2 = PCG64::seed(seed, inc);
[316](https://docs.rs#316)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[317](https://docs.rs#317)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_u64(), r2.next_u64());
[318](https://docs.rs#318)                assert_eq!(r1.rand_i64(), r2.next_u64() as i64);
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            }
[320](https://docs.rs#320)        }
[321](https://docs.rs#321)    }
[322](https://docs.rs#322)
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    #[test]
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    fn test_float32() {
[325](https://docs.rs#325)        {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)            let seed = 2718281828;
[327](https://docs.rs#327)            let mut r1 = Rand32::new(seed);
[328](https://docs.rs#328)            let mut r2 = PCG32::seed(seed, Rand32::DEFAULT_INC);
[329](https://docs.rs#329)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[330](https://docs.rs#330)                // First just make sure they both work with randomize's
[331](https://docs.rs#331)                // f32 conversion function -- sanity checks.
[332](https://docs.rs#332)                let i1 = r1.rand_u32();
[333](https://docs.rs#333)                let i2 = r2.next_u32();
[334](https://docs.rs#334)                assert_eq!(i1, i2);
[335](https://docs.rs#335)                let f1 = randomize::f32_half_open_right(i1);
[336](https://docs.rs#336)                let f2 = randomize::f32_half_open_right(i2);
[337](https://docs.rs#337)                // We can directly compare floats 'cause we do no math, it's
[338](https://docs.rs#338)                // literally the same bitwise algorithm with the same inputs.
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                assert_eq!(f1, f2);
[340](https://docs.rs#340)
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                // Make sure result is in [0.0, 1.0)
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                assert!(f1 >= 0.0);
[343](https://docs.rs#343)                assert!(f1 < 1.0);
[344](https://docs.rs#344)            }
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)            // At least make sure our float's from rand_float() are in the valid range.
[347](https://docs.rs#347)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[348](https://docs.rs#348)                let f1 = r1.rand_float();
[349](https://docs.rs#349)                assert!(f1 >= 0.0);
[350](https://docs.rs#350)                assert!(f1 < 1.0);
[351](https://docs.rs#351)            }
[352](https://docs.rs#352)
[353](https://docs.rs#353)            /*
[354](https://docs.rs#354)            TODO: Randomize changed its int-to-float conversion functions and now they don't
[355](https://docs.rs#355)            match ours.
[356](https://docs.rs#356)            for _ in 0..1000 {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)                // Now make sure our own float conversion function works.
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                let f1 = r1.rand_float();
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                //let f2 = randomize::f32_half_open_right(r2.next_u32());
[360](https://docs.rs#360)                let f2 = randomize::f32_open(r2.next_u32());
[361](https://docs.rs#361)                assert_eq!(f1, f2);
[362](https://docs.rs#362)                assert!(f1 >= 0.0);
[363](https://docs.rs#363)                assert!(f1 < 1.0);
[364](https://docs.rs#364)            }
[365](https://docs.rs#365)            */
[366](https://docs.rs#366)        }
